To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
• The ageing population is increasing in many parts of the world.
older adults’ experiences of sport and physical activity are complex, and are influenced by the interplay of social, political and cultural factors, as well as by their own personal experiences.
The media and policy documents promote the benefits of physical activity to the older population and encourage them to engage in active ageing.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ways in which older people are represented in the mass media and in popular culture.
the social construction of ageing and the ways in which sport, physical culture and physical activity are being used as a tool to manage and control the ageing body.
the ways in which sport and physical activity are used to construct, maintain and challenge the social order.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
active ageing is a myth.
the current discourse of active ageing is a form of ‘ageist’ rhetoric which is both harmful and dangerous.
sport and exercise is good for you, and you should do it!
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ‘agequake’ is not only about the numbers of older people but the way in which they have become the subject of an ‘ageist’ gaze.
the promotion of physical activity in older people is not a neutral process.
sport and active ageing is not a panacea for ageing societies.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we need to stop trying to stop ageing and instead focus on how to make ageing better.
older adults are not just a group to be managed but are a group of people who are active, have a lot to offer and are not a burden on the younger generation.
we need to move beyond the rhetoric of active ageing, and towards an approach that is more sensitive to the needs and aspirations that older persons themselves have for their later years of life.
